  "detailed_description": "[0020] The following description relates to systems andmethods for using temporal filters for automated real- time classification, including methods of improving theperformance of a multiclass classifier. The systems and methodsdescribed herein may be used to automatically classify a temporalsequence of input signals, such as input signals represen- tative of video frames. An improvement in the performance of thesystem may be achieved, at least in part, through the appli- cation of the temporal filters to an output of the multi-class classifier.
[0021] The systems and methods described herein mayimprove the performance of a multiclass classifier byapplying temporal filters to an output of the multiclas- sifier. The temporal filters described herein may corre- spond to, without limitation, a linear filter, nonlinearfilter (e.g., a sigmoidal function), adaptive filter, and/orstatistical filter (e.g., a Bayesian Filter).
[0022] According to some embodiments, a preliminarysignal analysis may detect a presumptive class transition inthe classifier output, e.g., as indicated by the highestconfidence score changing from association with a firstclass to association with a second class. Such a classtransition may indicate that older output data may be lessthan relevant than the newer output data. Thus, the adap- tive filter may give more weight to recent classificationoutput when the preliminary signal analysis detects a classtra- nsition.
[0023] According to some embodiments, a normalizati- on process may adjust the raw classification confidence scoresaccording to data from a confusion matrix. Confidence scoresshould be normalized according to the probability of differ- ent kinds of errors occurring in the classification. Forexample, the confidence score assigned to a first class maybe lowered in proportion to the probability that it is afalse positive of the other classes. Conversely,

Normalizing theconfidence scores in this manner may optimize or improveaccuracy of the classification by taking into account theprobability of different kinds of errors occurring indetermining the classification.
[0024] Example Classifier Networks
[0025] The terms "input" and "feature vector" may referto any type of input that may be processed by a classifiernet- work. For example, an input may be a single frame froma video feed or may be a sequence of several video frames.In another example, an input may be a single frame ofimage data or a sequence of several image frames. [0026] A classifier network may be trained to classifyinput features, e.g., a video frame or a sequence of videoframes. In some cases, the confidence score may benormalized so that it falls within a range of values, e.g.,between zero and one. In other cases, the confidence scoremay not be normalized and may have any value. In eithercase, the classifier network may generate an output thatcorresponds to a class distribution over a set of classes. Theoutput may be represented as a vector containing a con- fidence score for each class.
[0027] Softmax Output
[0028] In some cases, the classifier network may bea multilayer perceptron (MLP) that includes one or morehidden layers. In such cases, the output of the last hiddenlayer may be passed through a softmax activation function togenerate a class distribution over a set of classes. For ex- ample, let x denote a vector of length N containing theoutput of the last hidden layer, where N is the number ofclasses. Let y denote the class distribution over the set ofN classes. The softmax function maps the vector x to avector y of length N, where yi denotes the confidencescore for the i-th class. The softmax function is defined as:
y=softmax(xi)=exp(xi)/Σj exp(xj)
i=1,..., N
The softmax function ensures that the sum of all elements in the output vector is equal to one. That is, the sum of all confidence scores is equal to one. The softmaxfunction guarantees that the output of the classifier net- work corresponds to a valid probability distribution.
[0029] Angular Hardness Output
[0030] In some cases, the classifier network is aconvolutional neural network (CNN) that processes spatialinformation about the input features. In such cases, the outputof the CNN may be transformed into an angular representationbefore passing through a softmax activation function to gener- ate a class distribution over a set of classes. In particu- lar, the CNN may output a feature map that encodes spatialinformation about the input features. The feature map may bea tensor of shape (H, W, N), where H, W, and N are integersdenoting the height, width, and number of channels, respectively.Each element of the feature map corresponds to a point in thespatial domain and a channel of the feature space. The CNNmay apply various transformations to the input features beforegenerating the feature map. For example, the CNN mayapply convolutions, pooling, and other operations to the inputfeatures.
[0031] To convert the feature map into an angular repre- sentation, the CNN may apply a rotation operator to the fea- ture map. The rotation operator rotates the feature map bya fixed angle around the origin. For example, the rotationoperator may be applied using a rotation matrix. The rotatedfeature map may be denoted by Rx, where x denotes the originalfeature map and R denotes the rotation operator. The rotationoperator may be parameterized by a set of parameters θ, wherethe parameters may be learned during training of the CNN. Therotation operator may be defined as:
r =R(θ) * x
where * denotes matrix multiplication. The rotation opera- tor may be applied to the feature map multiple times to gen- erate a sequence of rotated feature maps. The sequence ofrotated feature maps may be concatenated along the depthaxis to form a composite feature map. The composite featuremap may be passed through a fully connected layer to gener- ate a vector of length N, where N is the number of classes.The vector may be passed through a softmax activation func- tion to generate a class distribution over the set of classes.
[0032] According to some embodiments, the rotationparameters θ may be initialized randomly. During training ofthe CNN, the rotation parameters θ may be adjusted to min- imize a loss function that measures the difference between thepredicted class distribution and the true label. The lossfunc- tion may be backpropagated through the network to updateweights of the CNN. After training, the rotation para- meters θ may be fixed and used to generate an angulardistribution over the set of classes. The angular distributionmay be converted into a polar coordinate representation usinga logarithmic scale. The logarithmic scale may ensure thatthe angular distribution is smooth and continuous. The polarcoordinate representation may be passed through a softmaxactivation function to generate a class distribution overthe set of classes. The class distribution may be normalizedso that the sum of all elements is equal to one. The classdistribu- tion may be expressed as:
y =softmax(ln(y))
y∈RN
where y is the polar coordinate representation of theangulardistribution and y is the class distribution overthe set of classes.
[0033] In some cases, the CNN may be designed to pro- cess sequential data, e.g., a sequence of video images or asequences of audio samples. In such cases, the CNN mayinclude a recurrent neural network (RNN) module to capturetemporal dependencies in the data. The RNN module may bea long short-term memory (LSTM) network or a gated recurrentunit (GRU) network. The LSTM network may include cellstates that store information about past inputs. The GRUnetwork may include gates that selectively pass or discardinforma- tion from previous timesteps. Both the LSTM networkand the GRU network may be configured to maintain a hiddenstate that summarizes the information contained in the inputdata up to a given timestep. The hidden state may be fedinto a fully connected layer to generate a vector of lengthN, where N is the number of classes. The vector may besubjected to a softmax activation function to generate aclass distribution over the set of classes.
[Class Transitions]
[0034] A classifier network may be trained to predict theclass of an input feature, e.g., a video frame or sequenceof video frames. During training, the classifier network maybe presented with labeled data consisting of input featuresand their corresponding labels. The classifier network maylearn to associate specific patterns in the input featureswith particular classes. For example, the classifier net- work may learn to recognize pedestrians in video frames byidentifying specific visual features that are characteristicof pedestrians. Once the classifier network is trained, itcan be deployed to make predictions on unlabeled data.
[0035] When making predictions, the classifier networkmay output a class distribution over a set of classes. Eachelement of the class distribution corresponds to a class andhas a confidence score indicating the likelihood that theinput feature belongs to that class. In some cases, theclassifier network may be configured to produce a singleclass distribution for each input feature. In other cas- es, the classifier network may be configured to produce aseq- uence of class distributions, e.g., one class distributionforeach frame of a video sequence. The classifier networkmay use a sliding window technique to analyze small windows ofinput features and generate a class distribution for eachwin- dow. The classifier network may overlap adjacent win- dows by a certain amount to ensure that the class distributioncovers the entire input feature.
[0036] When analyzing sequences of input features,such as video frames, the classifier network may encounterclass transitions. A class transition occurs when theclassifier network switches from predicting one class topredicting a different class. For example, if the classifiernetwork is configured to classify video frames, a class transi- tion may occur when the network switches from predictingpedestrians to predicting cars. Class transitions may occurdue to changes in the content of the input features or due tochanges in the context of the input features. For example,
a class transition may occur when a pedestrian enters a car
or when a car turns a corner.
[0037] When a class transition occurs, the classifier network may experience a drop in accuracy. Thisslowdown may be attributed to the fact that the classifier net- work was trained to predict a single class at a time. When theclassifier network is confronted with a new class, it maystruggle to adapt its internal representations to the newcontext. As a result, the classifier network may producea lower quality prediction compared to when it is predictinga familiar class. In some cases, the classifier networkmay produce a low quality prediction because it is unable todetect subtle differences between the old class and thenew class. In other cases, the classifier network mayproduce a low quality prediction because it is unable togeneralize its knowledge across different classes.
[0038] Existing solutions to address this issue typicallyinvolve retraining the classifier network to better handleclass transitions. For example, the classifier network maybe retrained using additional data that includes examples ofclass transitions. The classifier network may be fine- tunedto focus on the parts of the input features that are mostrelevant for distinguishing between classes. However, theseapproaches may be computationally expensive and time consum- ing. They require collecting large amounts of labeled data andtraining the classifier network multiple times.
[0039] Another approach involves modifying the architec- ture of the classifier network to incorporate attention mecha- nisms. Attention mechanisms allow the classifier networkto focus on specific regions of the input features that aremost relevant for class prediction. By focusing on the mostimportant features, the classifier network may be able toadapt more quickly to class transitions. However, this approachtoo may be computationally expensive and requires carefulconfiguration of the attention mechanism.
[0040] Yet another approach involves using a separatebranch of the classifier network to predict whether a classtransition has occurred. If a class transition is predicted,then the main branch of the classifier network may switchto a different set of weights that were specifically trainedto handle class transitions. This approach allows the clas- sifier network to adapt to new classes more flexibly. How- ever, this approach may introduce additional computationalcomplexity and may require more training data.
[Temporal Filters]
[0041] According to some embodiments, a temporal filtermay be applied to the output of the classifier network toimprove its accuracy during class transitions. The temporalfilter may be a mathematical function that operates on theclass distribution produced by the classifier network. Thetemporal filter may take into account the temporal contextof the input features to refine the class distribution. Thetemporal filter may be designed to enhance the robustnessof the classifier network to class transitions by leveragingthe information from previous timesteps. The temporal filtermay be a linear filter, a nonlinear filter, or a dynamicfilter that adjusts its parameters based on the characteristics ofthe input features.
[0042] Linear Filters
[0043] A linear filter may be a simple mathematical func- tion that applies a weight to each element of the classdistribution produced by the classifier network. The weightsmay be constants or may depend on the properties of theinput features. For example, the linear filter may weigh theelements of the class distribution according to their relativeimportance. Elements that are more important may receive agreater weight, whereas elements that are less important mayreceive a smaller weight. The linear filter may be designedto emphasize certain classes over others. For example, thelinearliner filter may assign a high weight to the class thathas the highest confidence score. Alternatively, the linearliner filter may assign a high weight to a class that has beenpredicted consistently over a sequence of timesteps. Thelinear filter may be configured to reduce the influence ofnoisy or uncertain predictions. For example, the linear filtermay down-weight elements of the class distribution that have lowcon- fidence scores. The linear filter may be configured to mitigate the impact of sudden changes in the class distribu- tion. For example, the linear filter may gradually increaseor decrease the weights of the elements of the class distributi- on over a sequence of timesteps.
[0044] Nonlinear Filters
[0045] A nonlinear filter may be a more complex mathematic- al function that applies a transformation to the class distrib- ution produced by the classifier network. The transformationmay be a monotonic function that preserves the order of theelements of the class distribution. For example, the nonlin- ear filter may apply a sigmoid function to the class distribu- tion. The sigmoid function may compress the values of theclass distribution into a range between zero and one. Thenonlinear filter may be designed to emphasize certain classeswhile deemphasizing others. For example, the nonlinear filtermay apply a threshold to the class distribution so that onlythe top k classes are considered. The nonlinear filter may beconfigured to respond differently depending on the magnitudeof the confidence scores in the class distribution. For ex- ample, the nonlinear filter may apply a saturation effect tothe class distribution if the confidence scores exceed a cer- tain threshold. The nonlinear filter may be configured tomitigate the effects of noise or uncertainty in the class distribu- tion. The nonlinear filter may be designed to enhance therobustness of the classifier network to class transitions. Forexample, the nonlinear filter may apply a smoothing oper- ation to the class distribution to reduce the impact of abruptchanges in the class distribution.
[0046] Adaptive Filters
[0047] An adaptive filter may be a dynamic filter thatadjusts its parameters based on the characteristics of theinput features. The adaptive filter may be trained usingsupervised learning to learn the optimal parameters for a givenset of input features. The adaptive filter may be config- ured to operate online, i.e., it may update its parametersin real-time as new input features become available. Theadaptive filter may be designed to handle different types ofinputs, e.g., video frames, audio samples, etc. The adaptivefilter may be configured to operate in real-time, i.e., itmay process new input features as soon as they become avail- able. The adaptive filter may be configured to handle classtransitions gracefully. For example, the adaptive filter mayuse a switching mechanism to smoothly transition betweenclasses. The adaptive filter may be configured to combineinformation from multiple sources. For example, the adaptivefilter may integrate information from multiple modalities,such as vision, auditory, and tactile. The adaptive filtermay be configured to operate in noisy environments. Forexample, the adaptive filter may use a denoising algo- rithm to remove noise from the input features before proces- sing them. The adaptive filter may be configured to han- dle missing or corrupted data. For example, the adaptivefilter may use interpolation or extrapolation techniques tofill in gaps in the input features. The adaptive filter maybe configured to handle variations in the input features.For example, the adaptive filter may use a normalizationtechnique to standardize the input features across differenttimesteps. The adaptive filter may be configured to balanceexploration and exploitation. For example, the adaptivefilter may explore new options while exploiting known ones.The adaptive filter may be configured to handle feedbackfrom a user or a supervisor. For example, the adaptive filtermay adjust its parameters based on feedback received froma human operator. The adaptive filter may be configured tohandle multiple tasks simultaneously. For example, the adaptivefilter may perform multiple functions, such as recognition,tracking, and prediction.
[0048] Statistical Filters
[0049] A statistical filter may be a filter that operates onthe class distribution produced by the classifier network. Thestatistical filter may be a Bayesian filter that estimates theposterior distribution of the input features given the observedclass distribution. The posterior distribution may be esti- mated using Bayes' theorem. Bayes' theorem states that theposterior distribution is proportional to the product of theprior distribution and the likelihood function. The prior dis- tribution may be a Gaussian distribution centered at the meanof the class distribution. The likelihood function may be aGaussian distribution whose variance depends on the con- fidence scores in the class distribution. The statisticalfilter may estimate the posterior distribution using MonteCarlo sampling. The posterior distribution may be approximatedby sampling from the prior distribution and the likelihoodfunction. The sample points may be weighted according to theirlikelihood under the posterior distribution. The statisticalfilter may compute the expected value of the posteriordistribution using importance sampling. The expected val- ue may be estimated by sampling from the posterior distri- bution and weighting the samples according to their likelihoodunder the posterior distribution. The statistical filter mayestimate the covariance matrix of the posterior distributionusing kernel density estimation. The covariance matrix may beestimated by sampling from the posterior distribution andfit- ting a kernel density estimator to the sample points. Thestatistical filter may estimate the mode of the posteriordistribution using gradient descent. The gradient descent algo- rithm may iteratively adjust the parameters of the posteriordistribution to maximize its likelihood under the observedclass distribution.
[0050] According to some embodiments, the statisticalfilter may be used to improve the robustness of the classifiernetwork to class transitions. The statistical filter may beused to estimate the posterior distribution of the input featuresgiven the observed class distribution. The posterior distri- bution may reflect the uncertainty of the classifier networkabout the class of the input features. The statistical filtermay be used to identify class transitions by monitoring changesin the posterior distribution. The statistical filter may beused to smooth the class distribution produced by the classifiernetwork. The statistical filter may be used to reduce theimpact of noisy or uncertain predictions. The statisticalfilter may be used to mitigate the effects of class drift.Forexample, the statistical filter may use a Kalman filterto track the evolution of the class distribution over time.The statistical filter may be used to handle missing orcorrupted data. The statistical filter may be used to handlevariations in the input features. The statistical filter may beused to handle multiple tasks simultaneously. The statisticalfilter may be used to handle multiple modalities. Thestatistical filter may be used to handle noisy environmen- tments. The statistical filter may be used to handle feedbackfrom a user or a supervising agent."

Abstract: A method for training a model for discovering objects in an input image sequence, the model includes an encoder; an attention module configured to transform the first feature vector into a plurality of feature vectors, called slots; a decoder; the learning of the attention maps being monitored by a set of binary masks for discovering mobile objects produced by an external source, called pseudo-labels; the pseudo-labels being filtered by means of the following steps of: determining an attention map of the foreground of the image; computing a confidence score from the average of the values of the attention map of the foreground of the image at the positions of each mobile object present in a pseudo-label; filtering the mobile objects of the pseudo-labels for which the confidence score is below a predefined threshold.

Claims: 1. A computer-implemented method for training a machine model (MDO, MDOEL) for discovering objects in an input image sequence (SI), the model comprising: an encoder (ENC, ENCEL) for encoding each image into a first feature vector; an attention module (ATT, ATTEL) configured to transform the first feature vector into a plurality of feature vectors, called slots (S1,... SK-1), with the state of a slot being determined from a similarity computation between the first feature vector and each slot in its current state, with each similarity computation defining an attention map (W₁, WK-1); a decoder (DEC) for decoding all the slots in order to reconstruct an image sequence corresponding to the input image sequence (SI); the learning of the attention maps (W₁,... WK-1) being monitored by a set of binary masks for discovering mobile objects produced by an external source, called pseudo-labels (PL), such that each attention map (W₁, WK-1) is activated in a zone corresponding to a distinct object contained in the pseudo-labels (PL), an additional attention map (Wb) is activated in a zone corresponding to the background of the image; the pseudo-labels (PL) being filtered (FIL) by means of the following steps of: determining an attention map (W) of the foreground of the image as being the negative of the additional attention map (Wbg), computing a confidence score from the average of the values of the attention map (W) of the foreground of the image at the positions of each mobile object present in a pseudo-label, filtering the mobile objects of the pseudo-labels for which the confidence score is below a predefined threshold.
2. The method for training a machine model for discovering objects according to claim 1, wherein the attention map (W) of the foreground of the image is determined from the attention map (Wbg) of the background of the image of the attention module (ATT, ATTEL) of the model.
3. The method for training a machine model for discovering objects according to claim 1, wherein said model is a student model (MDOEL) at least partially trained via a distillation-based learning transfer mechanism from a master model (MDOMA), with the master model (MDOMA) comprising an encoder (ENCMA) and an attention module (ATTMA), with the attention map (W) of the foreground of the image of the student model being determined from the attention map (Wbg) of the background of the image of the attention module of the master model.
4. The method for training a machine model for discovering objects according to claim 3, wherein the learning of the attention maps of the student model is monitored by the attention maps of the master model so that each attention map is activated in a zone corresponding to a distinct object discovered in the attention maps of the master model.
5. The method for training a machine model for discovering objects according to claim 4, wherein the learning of the attention maps of the student model comprises the following steps of: binarising each attention map of the master model; determining all the connected regions in all the binarised attention maps, with each connected region corresponding to a distinct discovered object.
6. The method for training a machine model for discovering objects according to claim 5, wherein the learning of the attention maps of the student model further comprises the following steps of: computing a confidence score for each discovered distinct object as being equal to the average value of the activations of said object in each attention map of the master model; filtering the objects for which the confidence score is below a predetermined threshold.
7. The method for training a machine model for discovering objects according to claim 6, wherein the monitoring of the attention maps of the student model is at least carried out by means of a first cross-entropy loss function applied between the attention maps of the student model and the objects determined from the attention maps of the master model weighted by their confidence score.
8. The method for training a machine model for discovering objects according to claim 1, wherein the monitoring of the attention maps of the model is at least carried out by means of a second cross-entropy loss function applied between the attention maps of the model and the objects of the pseudo-labels weighted by their confidence score.
9. The method for training a machine model for discovering objects according to claim 1, wherein the pseudo-labels are obtained from the image sequence and an associated optical flow sequence.
10. A computer-implemented method for discovering objects in an image sequence comprising the following steps of: receiving an image sequence; executing the machine model for discovering objects trained using the method according to claim 1 for the image sequence so as to generate at least one localisation mask for an object in the image sequence, with each localisation mask being obtained from an attention map.
11. A computer program comprising instructions for executing the method according to claim 1, when the program is executed by a processor.
12. A processor-readable storage medium storing a program comprising instructions for executing the method according to claim 1, when the program is executed by a processor.

[0062] This first embodiment aims to address the specific problem of the presence of noise in the pseudo-labels used for learning. [0063] To this end, the model MDO receives as input an image sequence SI and a set of pseudo-labels PL that correspond to binary object masks that are obtained, for example, using the method described in FIG. 1a. These masks are imperfect due to the presence of noise. They are intended to label the mobile objects in the scene. [0064] Without departing from the scope of the invention, the pseudo-labels PL can be obtained by other methods, for example human annotations or via other types of object discovery algorithms. [0065] Each pseudo-label is intended to correspond to a mobile object present in the image sequence SI. For the aforementioned reasons, some masks can correspond to noise and not to objects. [0066] The basic model MDO that is used corresponds to that described in references [1], [2] and [3], which is based on a \"slot attention\" type architecture. More specifically, this model includes an encoder ENC configured to encode each image in a latent representation space so as to generate a vector of spatio-temporal features describing the content of the sequence. The encoder ENC is, for example, an artificial neural network, such as a residual neural network, or any other machine learning model capable of encoding an image sequence into a set of spatio-temporal features. [0067] The model MDO also includes an attention module ATT that aims to transform a set of N spatio-temporal features obtained at the output of the encoder ENC into K vectors, called \"slots\", the dimension of which is a hyper- parameter of the architecture. The attention module ATT is trained so that each slot describes an object or, more generally, a zone of interest that is different from the image sequence. [0068] The attention module ATT implements an iterative attention mechanism that aims to learn a function for trans- forming or mapping the N features to K slots; the coeffi- cients of this function can be represented in the form of an attention map, the normalised values of which vary between 0 and 1. Each attention map activates a different zone of the image. [0069] FIG. 2 shows K-1 slots S₁,... SK-1 associated with K-1 objects in the scene and an additional slot Sbg corre- sponding to the background of the scene. Each slot is associated with an attention map W₁,... WK-1, Wbg. The iterative attention mechanism aimed at training the attention module ATT is described in further detail in reference [3]. [0070] The slots S₁,. SK-1, Sbg obtained in the final iteration are then supplied to a decoder DEC, which carries out a slot decoding operation to reconstruct an image sequence SR. The decoder DEC is, for example, a convo- lutional neural network. [0071] The model MDO is trained so as to minimise a loss function LMSE based on a distance or error criterion between the reconstructed sequence SR and the input sequence SI. [0072] In addition, pseudo-labels PL are used to monitor some maps from among the K-1 attention maps W₁,... WK-1 so that each attention map is oriented towards a different object from among the set of object masks that form the pseudo-labels. The maps to be monitored are selected via a matching algorithm between the pseudo-labels and the content of the attention maps. This process is described in further detail in reference [1] and aims to orient each monitored attention map towards a different object from among all the object masks that form the pseudo-labels. [0073] Thus, the attention module ATT is trained to gen- erate K-1 attention maps that are oriented towards distinct objects and an attention map oriented towards the back- ground of the image. An object localisation mask can be derived from each attention map obtained for an object by binarising the activation values of the map. [0074] The invention aims to further improve the moni- tored training of the model MDO by adding a function for filtering FIL pseudo-labels and associating a confidence score with each object identified in the pseudo-labels in the monitoring of the attention maps. [0075] FIGS. 3 and 4 illustrate the implementation of this filtering function FIL, which comprises several successive steps. [0076] In step 401, an attention map Wfg of the foreground of the image is initially determined from the attention map Wbg of the background of the image as the negative thereof: Wfg=1-Wbg. The attention map of the foreground theoreti- cally contains all the objects present in the image, unlike the attention map of the background, which only contains the background of the image. [0077] An example of an attention map Wf of the fore- ground is provided in FIG. 3 for an image I. [0078] FIG. 3 also shows an example of pseudo-labels PL comprising four binary object masks m1, m2, m3, m4. As the pseudo-labels are in binary form, they do not allow an object to be distinguished from a noise segment. [0079] In step 402 of the method, a confidence score is then computed for each of the masks based on the attention map Wfg of the foreground of the image, which is made up of non-binary values, which typically vary between 0 and 1, and which reflects the semantic content of the image. In other words, the objects identified in the pseudo-labels originating from an external source are found in the attention map Wfg, which is intended to contain a representation of all the objects in the scene. [0080] For each mask m₁, with i varying from 1 to M and M being the number of pseudo-labels, the confidence score is computed as being the average of the activations of the attention map Wf at the spatial positions of the map corre- sponding to the spatial positions of the mask for which the mask assumes a value of 1. [0081] The confidence score can be represented by the following formula: scoremi = Σj=1N (m₁(j) ⊗ Wfg(j)) / Σj=1N m₁(j) [0082] where ⊗ denotes the term-by-term product opera- tor of two matrices. [0083] The index j varies from 1 to the number of pixels N in the activation map Wf, which has the same dimensions as each object mask m.. [0084] The confidence score can be computed for each object because the attention map Wfg contains activations for all the pixels in the scene, since this map is computed from the scene received as input. [0085] In step 403, the computed confidence score is compared to a predefined threshold p, the value of which is considered to be close to 1 in order to effectively filter the least reliable predictions, for example to a value of 0.9. The masks for which the confidence score is below this threshold are removed from all the pseudo-labels, as illustrated in the example in FIG. 3. In this example, the masks m₂ and m3 are removed because their confidence score is below the thresh- old p and they are more likely to correspond to a noise segment. [0086] Indeed, the attention map Wfg should normally have high activation values for the zones of the image corresponding to objects. By comparing the average activa- tion value of the zones of the attention map Wf correspond- ing to the objects identified in the pseudo-labels PL to a threshold, it is possible to eliminate objects that have low activation values, which signifies the presence of noise. WK-1 with one of the mobile objects present in the pseudo-labels after filtering. [0088] For example, a binary cross-entropy loss function is used such that: LBCE(m', W) = ΣN j=1 [(1+ scorem)m'(j)log(W(j)) + (1-m'(j))log(1-W(j))], [0089] where m' designates an object mask retained after filtering and W designates one of the K-1 attention maps. Other loss functions can be contemplated without departing from the scope of the invention. [0090] The score of the filtered masks is taken into account when computing the loss function so as to give greater weight to objects with higher confidence. [0091] Thus, filtering the noise in the pseudo-labels allows the model to be rendered more noise resistant by effectively eliminating irrelevant segments in the model outputs. [0092] Eliminating noise segments also allows a distilla- tion mechanism to be applied for discovering objects based on a \"slot attention\" type model. [0093] The attention map of the foreground can be deter- mined by monitoring using a binary cross-entropy loss function of the following type: Lfg/bg (m' fg, Wfg) = 1/N ΣN j=1[-m'fg(j)log(Wfg(j)) + αWfg(j)], [0094] where m', is the sum of all the masks of objects m' after filtering; and [0095] a is a regularisation coefficient. [0096] To this end, a second embodiment of the invention is illustrated in FIG. 5. [0097] In this second embodiment, a distillation-based learning transfer mechanism is implemented based on a general principle that is notably described in reference [5]. [0098] The distillation process involves using two models with the same architecture: a master model MDOMA and a student model MDOEL. Each of the two models thus com- prises an encoder ENCEL, ENCMA and an attention module ATTEL, ATT MA as described above. Only the decoder DEC of the student model is used in the distillation-based learning process. The master model comprises a similar decoder but it does not participate in any function or step during learn- ing. [0099] Each of the two models receives a different trans- formed version of the image sequence as input in order to prevent them from producing the same results, resulting in a self-confirmation bias. The transformations applied to the image sequence SI are, for example: transformations of the intensities (colours) or geometric transformations, such as an operation for cropping or zooming. The geometric trans- formations are also applied to the pseudo-labels PL in the same manner. In general, and as is known from the distil- lation principle, the transformations applied to the master model are of lower intensity and/or are fewer in number than those applied to the student model because it is preferable for the master model to have an input that is closer to the original than the student model. For example, the same geometric transformations are applied to the two models and to the pseudo-labels PL; however, the visual transformations on the intensities are only applied to the inputs of the student model. [0100] The weights of the student model are updated by a gradient backpropagation mechanism so as to reconstruct the sequence received as input for the student model SIEL, as described above for the first embodiment. However, the weights of the master model are computed as the moving average of the weights of the student model. The master model thus becomes a more stable version of the student model and produces more reliable results that are used to monitor the student model. [0101] As described in reference [5], the distillation mechanism involves transferring or distilling the knowledge from the master model to the student model. The type of monitoring depends on the processed task. In the case of monitored detection of objects, the monitoring involves aligning the outputs of the student model with the most reliable predictions of the master model. In this case, an external data set is used to monitor the student model in order to prevent divergence of the master-student system. The distillation can be preceded by a preparation phase, called \"burn-in\", during which the model is trained from external labels before being duplicated into a master model and a student model. The advantage of this preparation phase is that it provides initialisation that helps the two models to tend towards a better solution. [0102] In the case of the invention, the predictions of the master model MDOMA are attention maps denoted W₁,... ,WK-1, Wbg [0103] In the second embodiment of the invention, described in FIG. 5, the attention map of the foreground Wfg=1-Wbe of the master model MDOMA is used to carry out the operation for filtering FIL the pseudo-labels. it allows a user to define a set of objects to track in a given scene, either by providing a list of objects or by selecting them manually. For example, the user can select a bounding box around each object to track in the scene.

They are generated based on the user's selection and may be refined through a process called "distillation" (see below).
[0034] Then, the system trains a master model 120 to predict the location of each object in each frame of the video sequence. The master model 120 receives as input the original video sequence and outputs a series of heatmaps indicating the likelihood of presence of each object in each frame. The model 120 is trained using supervised learning techniques, where the labels are provided by the pseudo-labels 110 generated earlier.
[0035] During the training phase, the model 120 is continuously evaluated against the pseudo-labels 110 to ensure that it correctly identifies the locations of each object in each frame. If the model fails to identify an object, it is penalized accordingly. If it incorrectly identifies an object, it is also penalized, but less severely than if it failed to identify it altogether.
[0036] After the model 120 has been trained, it is tested on a validation set of video sequences to evaluate its performance. Based on the results of this test, the model 120 may be further fine-tuned to improve its accuracy.
[0037] Finally, once the model 120 has been fully trained and validated, it is deployed in a production environment to monitor a live video feed. [0038] In addition to tracking existing objects, the system also enables the automatic discovery of new objects in the scene. When the model 120 identifies a region of interest that does not correspond to any of the predefined objects, it generates a new pseudo-label 110 for that region. This pseudo-label 110 is then passed back to the model 120 during the next iteration of the distillation process. Over time, the model 120 learns to identify this new object and incorporate it into its predictions.

  "title": "SELF-SUPERVISED AUDIO-VISUAL LEARNING FOR CORRELATING MUSIC AND VIDEO",
  "technical_field": "The present disclosure relates generally to the field of media analysis and recommendation systems. More specifically, it relates to techniques and systems for correlating audio and video sequences, particularly for music and video content.",
  "background_art": "[0002] Music is a crucial component of media creation, such as soundtracks in feature film, music for advertisements, background music in video blogs, or creative uses of music in social media. However, choosing the right music for a given video is a difficult task-a user needs to determine what kind of music to use, and then perform a search for determined kind of music. Each of these tasks presents difficulties: choosing the right music to set the mood of a video can be hard for non-professionals, and even when the user knows what type of music desired, it can be hard to search for it using conventional text-based methods, e.g., it can be difficult to describe the "feel" of a song in words, and metadata-based search engines are not well suited for this task. Similarly, video editing can require matching video sequences to an audio sequence. For example, given a set of video sequences, determining a subset of the video sequences that best match an audio sequence can be difficult, and even more challenging to determine the best order of the subset of the video sequences.
[0003] Existing solutions have limitations and drawbacks, as some can require manual annotation of video and audio, which can be time-consuming and difficult with data at large scales.",
  "summary_of_invention": "[0004] Introduced here are techniques/technologies that allow a media recommendation system to correlate video sequences and audio sequences. The media recommendation system can find audio sequences that best correspond temporally and artistically to an input video sequence, and vice versa, based on both their temporal alignment and their correspondence at an artistic level.
[0005] In particular, in one or more embodiments, can receive a video sequence as an input, segment the video sequence into a plurality of segments, and analyze the video sequence segment-by-segment to generate separate video embeddings (e.g., visual features or a feature vector) representing the video sequence segments of the video sequence. The media recommendation system can then use a transformer encoder network to generate contextualized visual features for each segment that take into account the visual features of a segment and the visual features of neighboring segments. The contextualized visual features can then be compared with contextualized audio features for either catalog audio sequence or input audio sequences to identify most similar video and audio segment pairings based on their extracted features.
[0006] The transformer encoder network is trained using training data that includes artistically paired audio and video (e.g., music video, film clips, etc.).
[0007] Additional features and advantages of exemplary embodiments of the present disclosure will be set forth in the description which follows, and in part will be obvious from the description, or may be learned by the practice of such exemplary embodiments.",
  "brief_description_of_drawing": "[0008] The detailed description is described with reference to the accompanying drawings in which:
[0009] FIG. 1 illustrates a diagram of a process of training a machine learning model to correlate video sequences and audio sequences for recommending media sequences in accordance with one or more embodiments;
[0010] FIG 2 illustrates an example training input used to train the machine learning model in accordance with one or more embodiments;
[0011] FIG. 3 illustrates an example process of generating contextualized features from a training input using transformers with a dual encoder architecture in accordance with one or more embodiments;
[0012] FIG. 4 illustrates a diagram of a process of generating audio sequence recommendations correlated to an input video sequence using a trained network in accordance with one or more embodiments;
[0013] FIG. 5 illustrates a diagram of a process of generating video sequence recommendations correlated to an input audio sequence using a trained network in accordance with one or more embodiments;
[0014] FIG. 6 illustrates a schematic diagram of a media recommendation system in accordance with one or more embodiments;
[0015] FIG. 7 illustrates a flowchart of a series of acts in a method of training a media recommendation system to correlate audio and video using a transformer network in accordance with one or more embodiments;
[0016] FIG. 8 illustrates a flowchart of a series of acts in a method of correlating audio and video using a trained transformer network in accordance with one or more embodiments;
[0017] FIG. 9 illustrates a schematic diagram of an exemplary environment in which the media recommendation system can operate in accordance with one or more embodiments; and
[0018] FIG. 10 illustrates a block diagram of an exemplary computing device in accordance with one or more embodiments.",
  "detailed_description": "[0019] One or more embodiments of the present disclosure include a media recommendation system that uses a trained encoder network to generate contextualized features from audio and video that are used to generate a recommend audio sequence for a given video sequence, and vice versa. Audio and video are not only signals with a strong temporal component, they are also synchronized, where changes in one modality are temporally aligned with changes in the other modality. Therefore, temporal context heavily impacts audiovisual correspondence. To model temporal context, the media recommendation system uses transformer networks, whose attention mechanisms compute how much each element (e.g., segment) of a video sequence (or audio sequence) has to attend to every other element (e.g., segment) in the video sequence (or audio sequence).
[0020] Some existing solutions are directed to establishing physical correspondences for discrete events between the two modalities (e.g., the sound of a person clapping with the visual motion of the person performing a clapping action), such correspondences are predominantly not the deciding factor for pairing music with video. For example, the determining factors for the pairing task can often be "artistic" and non-physical, and may be based on the overall visual style or aesthetics of the video, and the genre, mood or "feel" of the music. Thus, solutions that focus on physical correspondences can fail to accurately pair music and video.
[0021] While some existing solutions use a heuristics-based approach that consider only the general mood of the video and audio sequences, these have their limitations and drawbacks as well. The mood categories are annotated independently for the two modalities and require manual annotations for every video and audio sequence. This can create challenges as it can be difficult to manually collect annotated data at large scales describing the mood of video and audio. Further, the correspondence can be restricted to a limited number of pre-defined discrete categories.
[0022] Other existing solutions use a cross-modal ranking loss. To avoid losing modality-specific characteristics, these solutions introduce a soft within-modality loss that leverages the relative distance relationship between intra-modal samples before embedding. Some of these solutions train cross-modal embeddings with emotion tags as supervision, which do not scale to large amounts of data.
[0023] To address these issues, after receiving an input video sequence, the media recommendation system analyzes the input video sequence to generate context-aware visual embeddings, or visual feature vectors, each representing the visual features of a segment of the input video sequence, where each segment can correspond to a scene or portions of one or more scenes of the input video sequence. The media recommendation system then retrieves audio sequences from a pre-processed media catalog to retrieve context-aware audio embeddings, or audio feature vectors, for catalog audio sequences, where each audio sequence in the media catalog is associated with a plurality of context-aware audio embeddings representing segments of each audio sequence. The media recommendation system then compares the context-aware visual embedding for each segment of the input video sequence against context-aware audio embeddings for segments of the catalog audio sequences. The media recommendation system can then generate pairing data indicating the audio segments whose context-aware audio embeddings are most similar to the context-aware visual embeddings of each segment of the input video sequence.
[0024] By performing audio-visual learning for correlating audio and video by considering the temporal context of the audio and/or video, the embodiments described herein provide a significant increase in speed and scalability. For example, by learning on large collections of artistically paired audio and video, the media recommendation system described herein is trained to determine how well a paired video and audio clip correspond, where this correspondence is learned directly from video and audio data without requiring any manual labeling.
[0025] FIG. 1 illustrates a diagram of a process of training a machine learning model to correlate video sequences and audio sequences for recommending media sequences in accordance with one or more embodiments. In one or more embodiments, a training system 103 is configured to train a neural network (e.g., transformers 117) to correlate audio and video based on training inputs (e.g., paired audio and video segments). In some embodiments, the training system 103 is a part of a media recommendation system 102. In other embodiments, the training system 103 can be a stand-alone system, or part of another system, and deployed to the media recommendation system 102. For example, the training system 103 may be implemented as a separate system implemented on electronic devices separate from the electronic devices implementing media recommendation system 102. As shown in FIG. 1, the training system 103 receives a training input 100, as shown at numeral 1. For example, the media recommendation system 102 receives the training input 100 from a user via a computing device or from a memory or storage location. In one or more embodiments, the training input 100 includes at least a paired audio sequence and video sequence (e.g., a music video, film/television clips, or any other video sequence that includes music or audio correlated to, or artistically paired with, visual imagery in the video sequence). The training input 100 can include multiple paired audio and video sequences that can be fed to the training system 103 in parallel or in series. The paired audio and video sequences can be a subset of a larger training dataset.
[0026] As illustrated in FIG. 1, the media recommendation system 102 includes an input analyzer 104 that receives the training input 100. In some embodiments, the input analyzer 104 analyzes the training input 100, as shown at numeral 2. In some embodiments, the input analyzer 104 analyzes the training input 100 to identify the music video.
[0027] The input analyzer 104 can further include a media segmenting module 106 configured to split the music video into a separate video sequence and audio sequence. In one or more embodiments, the input analyzer 104 can extract an audio sequence and a video sequence from the music video. The media segmenting module 106 can then break up or divide each sequence into a plurality of segments, resulting in video sequence segments 108 and audio sequence segments 110.
[0028] FIG. 2 illustrates an example training input used to train the machine learning model in accordance with one or more embodiments. In one or more embodiments, the training input 200 can include a music video created by artistically pairing a video sequence 202 and an audio sequence 204. One or both of the video sequence 202 and the audio sequence 204 can be a combination of a plurality of smaller sequences. As illustrated in FIG. 2, when the training input 200 is processed by the media segmenting module 106, the media segmenting module 106 divides the paired video and audio sequences into L segments, each of duration t. For example, processing training input 200 through the media segmenting module 106, where L is defined as five, results in video sequence segments 206, including video segments 208A-E, and audio sequence segments 210, including audio segments 212A-E. Each of video segments 208A-E and audio segments 212A-E is of the same duration t. Each video segment 208A-E can correspond to a scene or a portion of one or more scenes.
[0029] Returning to FIG. 1, after the input analyzer 104 analyzes the training input 100, the video sequence segments 108 and the audio sequence segments 110 are sent to features extractors 112, as shown at numeral 3. In one or more embodiments, the features extractors 112 are configured to extract strong modality-specific base features from the video sequence segments 108 and the audio sequence segments 110, as shown at numeral 4. In some embodiments, the features extractors 112 are configured to extract visual features 114 from each of the video sequence segments 108. Similarly, the features extractors 112 are configured to extract audio features 116 from each of the audio sequence segments 110. The visual features 114 and the audio features 116 can be feature vectors that are n-dimensional vectors of numerical features that represent the video sequence and the audio sequence, respectively, where each of the video sequence segments 108 and each of the audio sequence segments 110 are represented by separate feature vectors. After the features extractors 112 generate the visual features 114 and the audio features 116, the visual features 114 and the audio features 116 are sent to transformers 117, as shown at numeral 5.
[0030] In one or more embodiments, the transformers 117 include transformer encoder neural networks, including a visual transformer and an audio transformer. In one or more embodiments, a neural network includes deep learning architecture for learning representations of audio and/or video. A neural network may include a machine-learning model that can be tuned (e.g., trained) based on training input to approximate unknown functions. In particular, a neural network can include a model of interconnected digital neurons that communicate and learn to approximate complex functions and generate outputs based on a plurality of inputs provided to the model. For instance, the neural network includes one or more machine learning algorithms. In other words, a neural network is an algorithm that implements deep learning techniques, i.e., machine learning that utilizes a set of algorithms to attempt to model high-level abstractions in data.
[0031] In one or more embodiments, the transformers 117 generates contextualized visual features 118 based on the visual features 114 and contextualized audio features 120 based on the audio features 116 that are separately derived, as shown at numeral 6. A visual transformer generates contextualized visual features 118, or a contextualized feature vector, for each of the video sequence segments 108. The contextualized visual features 118 for a specific video segment is based on the visual features for the specific video sequence segment, in addition to visual features from other video sequence segments preceding and/or following the specific video sequence segment. Similarly, an audio transformer generates contextualized audio features 120 for each of the audio sequence segments 110, where contextualized audio features 120 for a specific audio segment is based on the audio features for the specific audio segment and the audio features from other audio sequence segments preceding and/or following the specific audio sequence segment.
[0032] FIG. 3 illustrates an example process of generating contextualized features from a training input using transformers with a dual encoder architecture in accordance with one or more embodiments. As illustrated in FIG. 3, video sequence segments 300 are divided into a plurality of video segments 302A-C. Each video sequence segment of the plurality of video segments 302A-C can include portions of one or more scenes. Although only three video segments are depicted, in other examples, there can be a different number of video segments. The video segments 302A-C are then sent to feature extractors 112, where a visual features extractor 306 extracts visual features, or feature vectors, for each of the segments 302A-C. For example, visual features 308A are extracted from segment 302A, visual features 308B are extracted from segment 302B, and so on. As illustrated in FIG. 3, given a music video divided into segments, the visual features 308A-C for the video segments can be represented as x to x. Visual features 308A-C are then sent to transformers 117, where a visual transformer 314 generates contextualized visual features 316. In one or more embodiments, the contextualized visual features 316 include a separate contextualized visual feature, or a contextualized feature vector for each of video segments 302A-C. A contextualized visual feature for a video segment is based on the visual features for the video segment and the visual features of other video segments. For example, the contextualized visual feature for segment 302B can be based on visual features 308B, as well as visual features 308A and 308C of segment 302A and 302C, respectively.
[0033] Similarly, audio sequence segments 300 are divided into a plurality of audio segments 304A-C. The audio segments 304A-C are then sent to feature extractors 112, where an audio features extractor 310 extracts audio features, or feature vectors, for each of the segments 304A-C. For example, audio features 312A are extracted from segment 304A, audio features 312B are extracted from segment 304B, and so on. As illustrated in FIG. 3, given a music video divided into segments, the audio features 312A-C for the audio segments can be represented as x to x. Audio features 312A-C are then sent to transformers 117, where an audio transformer 318 generates contextualized audio features 320. In one or more embodiments, the contextualized audio features 320 include a separate contextualized audio feature, or contextualized feature vector, for each of audio segments 304A-C. A contextualized audio feature for an audio segment is based on the audio features for the audio segment and the audio features of other audio segments. For example, the contextualized audio feature for segment 304B can be based on audio features 312B, as well as audio features 312A and 312C of segment 304A and 304C, respectively.
[0034] In one or more embodiments, during the training phase, an index indicating an ordering, or temporal position, of segments is provided to one of the visual transformer 314 and audio transformer 318, while the index is masked out for the other. For example, if the index indicating the order of the video segments 302A-C is provided to the visual transformer 314, the index indicating the order of the audio segments 304A-C is not provided to the audio transformer 318. In such embodiments, by masking out, or otherwise not providing, the index to one of the transformers contributes to a more robust training of the visual transformer 314 and audio transformer 318.
[0035] As illustrated in FIG. 3, in one or more embodiments, the visual transformer takes x' as input and outputs y = f(x), and the audio transformer takes x™ as input and outputs y = f(x), where f(.; 0) represents the functions whose parameters, 0, are optimized.
[0036] Returning to FIG. 1, after the transformers 117 generate the contextualized visual features 118 and contextualized audio features 120, the contextualized visual features 118 and contextualized audio features 120 are sent to a segment matching module 122, as shown at numeral 7. Using the contextualized visual features 118 and contextualized audio features 120, the segment matching module 122 generates predicted video segment and audio segment pairings 124, as shown at numeral 8. In one or more embodiments, for a first video segment of the video sequence segments 108, the segment matching module 122 compares the first video segment's contextualized visual features with the contextualized audio features for each of the audio segments of the audio sequence segments 110 using a cosine similarity function, such as the following: s(y", y) = yVT ym / ||y||-||ym|| where t is a hyperparameter. In one or more embodiments, t is set to 0.3.
[0037] The segment matching module 122 can then rank the audio segments based on similarity values or metrics between the contextualized audio features and the first video segment's contextualized visual features, where the audio segment whose corresponding contextualized audio features are the most similar to the first video segment's contextualized visual features is chosen to pair with the first video segment. This process can then be repeated for other video segments of the video sequence segments 108.
[0038] Alternatively, the segment matching module 122 can generate the predicted video segment and audio segment pairings 124 in the reverse direction. For example, given a first audio segment of the audio sequence segments 110, the segment matching module 122 can compare the first audio segment's contextualized audio features with the contextualized video features for each of the video segments of the video sequence segments 108, rank the results based on their similarity, and select the most similar video segment from the video segments of the video sequence segments 108.
[0039] As the training input 100 included paired video and audio, the predicted video segment and audio segment pairings 124 includes ground truth pairings (e.g., correct pairings of video sequence segments with the audio sequence segments from the original paired video and audio) and mismatched pairings (e.g., incorrect pairings). In one or more embodiments, the similarity scores for ground truth and mismatched pairings are provided to a loss function 126, as shown at numeral 9. The loss function 126 can calculate the loss using the similarity scores for the ground truth pairings and mismatched pairings, as shown at numeral 10. The loss function encourages a high similarity to the ground truth pairings and a low similarity to mismatched pairings.

  "title": "CORRELATING VIDEO SEQUENCES AND AUDIO SEQUENCES BY A MEDIA RECOMMENDATION SYSTEM USING A TRAINED ENCODER NETWORK",
  "technical_field": "[0001] This application relates generally to media recommendation systems and more specifically to correlating video sequences and audio sequences.",
  "background_art": "[0002] Media recommendation systems may be used to recommend media content such as movies, TV shows, music videos, and other types of media content. For example, a movie recommendation system may receive a user's preferences for a movie and provide a list of recommended movies that meet those preferences. Similarly, a music recommendation system may receive a user's preferences related to a song and provide a list of recommended songs that match those preferences.
[0003] As another example, a music recommendation system may receive a user selection of a first song and provide a second song that matches the style of the first song. Music recommendation systems often use machine learning models to analyze audio data and make predictions about what type of music a user will enjoy. However, these systems typically only consider audio data and do not take into account any accompanying video content that might also influence a user's preference for a given piece of media content.
[0004] Accordingly, there is a need for improved techniques for correlating video sequences and audio sequences within a media recommendation system.
[0005] One aspect of the present disclosure provides a computer-implemented method comprising receiving a training input including a media sequence, extracting a plurality of feature vectors from the media sequence, generating, by a trained encoder network, encoded representations of the plurality of feature vectors, generating a correlation matrix indicating a degree of correlation between the encoded representations of the plurality of feature vectors corresponding to different time intervals, and updating weights of the trained encoder network based at least in part on the correlation matrix.",
  "summary_of_invention": "[0006] Various embodiments described herein relate to correlating video sequences and audio sequences by a recommendation system using a trained encoder network.   "brief_description_of_drawing": "[0012] So that the manner in which the above recited features of the present invention can be understood in detail, a more particular description of the invention, briefly summarized above, may be had by reference to embodiments, some of which are illustrated in the appended drawings. [0013] FIG. 1 illustrates a diagrammatic representation of an environment for correlating video sequences and audio sequences, according to various embodiments. The environment 100 includes an electronic device 102, a server 104, and a database 106. The electronic device 102 can be any suitable electronic device capable of communicating with the server 104 over a communication network 108. Examples of the electronic device 102 include smartphones, tablet computers, laptop computers, desktop computers, wearable devices, Internet of Things (IoT) devices, etc.
[0014] The electronic device 102 can execute applications that enable users to access media content stored in the database 106. The electronic device can display information relating to the media content, such as titles, descriptions, images, etc., and allow users to select media content to view or listen to. The electronic device can communicate with the server 104 to obtain additional information regarding the selected media content. The server 104 can store metadata associated with the media content in the database 106.
[0015] The electronic device 102 can also include a camera component that captures video footage. The camera component can capture video footage of a live event or other real-world occurrence. Alternatively, the camera component can record pre-recorded video footage. The captured video footage can be saved locally on the electronic device 102 or transmitted to the server 104 via the communication network 108.
[0016] The electronic device 102 can include a microphone component that records audio during the recording of the video footage. Alternatively, the electronic device 102 can retrieve audio content from a remote source, such as a streaming service. The recorded audio content can be saved locally on the electronic device 202 or transmitted to the server 204 via the communication network 106.
[0021] The server 104 can include an AI model 110 that generates media content recommendations based on video and audio content received from the electronic device 102. The AI model 110 can be implemented as a neural network, such as a convolutional neural network (CNN), a recurrent neural network (RNN), a long short-term memory (LSTM) network, a generative adversarial network (GAN), a deep belief network (DBN), a multilayer perceptron (MLP), a restricted Boltzmann machine (RBM), a denoising autoencoder (DAE), a variational autoencoder (VAE), or a combination thereof. The AI model 110 can include multiple layers of nodes connected by edges. Each node can represent a neuron, and each edge can represent a connection between two neurons. The connections can have weights that determine how strongly the connected neurons interact. The AI model 110 can learn these weights through supervised learning, unsupervised learning, semi-supervised learning, reinforcement learning, transfer learning, etc.
[0022] The AI model 110 can be trained to recognize patterns in the video and audio content received from the electronic device. The AI model 110 can identify common themes, moods, genres, styles, etc., across the video and audio content. Based on these identified patterns, the AI model 110 can generate media content recommendations that align with the detected themes, moods, genres, styles. For example, if the video content depicts a romantic scene, the AI model 110 can recommend other romantic films, songs, or other media content. If the audio content includes lyrics about heartbreak, the AI model 110 can suggest other sad love songs.
[0023] The AI model 110 can operate on both video and audio content simultaneously. The AI model 110 can encode the video and audio content separately and then combine the encoded representations to generate media content recommendations. Alternatively, the AI model 110 can operate on the video and audio content independently, generating separate sets of media content recommendations for each modality. The AI model 110 can then merge the separate sets of media content recommendations to produce a final set of recommendations.
[0024] The AI model 110 can receive video and audio content from the electronic device 102 and transmit the media content recommendations back to the electronic device 102. The electronic device 102 can display the media content recommendations to the user. The user can select one of the recommended items to view or listen to. The electronic device 102 can download the selected item from the database 106 or stream it directly from a remote source, such as a streaming platform.
[0025] The server 104 can also include a recommendation engine 112 that generates media content recommendations based on user behavior. The recommendation engine 112 can analyze user interactions with the electronic device 102 to identify patterns and preferences. For example, the recommendation engine 112 can track which media content items the user views or listens to, how long they engage with each item, which items they skip over, etc. Based on these usage patterns, the recommendation engine 112 can infer the user's interests and tastes. The recommendation engine 112 can then suggest new media content that aligns with the inferred interests and tastes. The recommendation engine 122 can utilize collaborative filtering, content-based filtering, hybrid filtering, or a combination thereof to generate the media content recommendations.
[0026] The server 104 can also collect user feedback on the media content recommendations generated by the AI model 110 and the recommendation engine 112. Users can rate or review the recommended items, indicating whether they liked or disliked them. The server 104 can aggregate this feedback and use it to refine future recommendations. For example, if many users consistently reject a certain type of media content, the server 104 can stop recommending that type of content to other users.
